title: The Baptismal Regeneration Controversy: Confronting the Church of England
seoTitle: The Baptismal Regeneration Controversy | Charles Spurgeon

content.text: Throughout his ministry, Charles Haddon Spurgeon never shied away from theological conflict when he believed the truth of the Gospel was at stake. However, few events in his career generated as much explosive backlash as the delivery of his sermon Baptismal Regeneration (Sermon No. 573) in 1864. Recognizing the gravity of the subject, Spurgeon deliberately confronted the established religious order of his day. The public response was unprecedented; the printed version of the sermon experienced a staggering demand, selling between 300,000 and 350,000 copies within a very short period, making it his most widely distributed individual sermon while he was alive. This singular message ignited a fierce controversy that reverberated throughout Victorian England and permanently altered Spurgeon's relationship with the Anglican establishment.
The Theological Heart of the Dispute

The core of the controversy centered on the Church of England's Book of Common Prayer, specifically its liturgy for infant baptism. Spurgeon quoted the prescribed form directly to his congregation, noting that after a few drops of water were sprinkled on an infant, the priest was instructed to say: "Seeing now, dearly beloved brethren, that this child is regenerate and grafted into the body of Christ’s Church, let us give thanks unto Almighty God for these benefits".

To Spurgeon, a staunch Reformed Baptist, this doctrine was a dangerous subversion of the Gospel. He emphatically declared that a physical ceremony could never produce a spiritual birth, and that the teaching of baptismal regeneration was a "deceitful invention of antichrist". He argued that believing faith and repentance are the absolute, indispensable requisites for salvation, whereas baptism is strictly a secondary, outward act of obedience—a public testimony to a spiritual work of grace that has already been completed inwardly.

What made Spurgeon's sermon particularly scandalous was not merely his theological disagreement, but his direct moral attack on the Evangelical clergymen within the Church of England. Spurgeon knew that many Evangelical Anglicans did not genuinely believe that water baptism regenerated infants, yet they continued to use the Book of Common Prayer and perform the ceremony to maintain their positions.

Spurgeon accused these ministers of gross equivocation and dishonesty, stating: "It is time that there should be an end put to the flirtations of honest men with those who believe one way and swear another. If men believe baptism works regeneration, let them say so. But if they do not so believe it in their hearts, and yet subscribe, and yet more, get their livings by subscribing to words asserting it, let them find congenial associates among men who can equivocate and shuffle". He refused to accept any theological compromise where men professed a faith they did not truly believe.

Furthermore, Spurgeon viewed the doctrine of baptismal regeneration—often associated with the Tractarian or Puseyite movement of his day—as the very essence and soul of Popery. He warned his congregation that this form of error was acting as a stepping stone, preparing the way for Roman Catholicism to reclaim England. Observing a rapid increase in the presence of monks, priests, and Catholic missions in London, Spurgeon argued that the Church of England was "gently and smoothly turfing the road, and making it as soft and smooth as possible, that converts may travel down to the nethermost hell of Popery". He believed that resting in ceremonies, altars, and fonts was fundamentally contrary to the Gospel of grace.

The fallout from the sermon was immediate and severe. Spurgeon was widely accused of being uncharitable and divisive. Prominent nonconformist and Anglican figures, including the respected minister Octavius Winslow, published direct responses condemning Spurgeon's heavy indictment against the Evangelical clergy. Consequently, the controversy cost Spurgeon dearly; several of his friends distanced themselves from him, and he experienced a painful degree of isolation.

Yet, he remained entirely unapologetic. When critics accused him of lacking Christian charity, Spurgeon defended himself by stating that he was merely delivering the message of his Master, who said, "Except a man be born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God". Believing that the time had come to end the "truce or parley" between God's servants and theological compromisers, Spurgeon gladly bore the cost of the controversy, proving that his ultimate allegiance was to the purity of the Gospel rather than to the preservation of superficial ecclesiastical unity.
